opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fiona. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course! I've got about half an hour before pick-up, so we're good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for writing newsletters to parents. That's about it in my room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is wiping noses, settling fights and teaching four-year-olds to share. No computer is doing that. What bothers me is the kids who arrive already glued to a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my classroom screen-free. Run a little evening session for parents on play and talking at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work. A bit sad about the screens.

S0.say: It's handy for writing newsletters to parents. That's about it in my room.
S0.think: No computer is wiping noses or teaching four-year-olds to share. Children glued to tablets bother her more.
S0.do: Keeps her classroom screen-free and runs an evening session for parents on play and talk.
S0.feel: Calm about work, a bit sad about the screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say little kids need people, not programs, and I'd keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still feels safe for me. Fewer beginners hired in offices might mean some parents struggle, but kindergarten carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. Maybe save a bit more, because we've got very little put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

S1.say: Little kids need people, not programs.
S1.think: Her job still feels safe, though some parents might struggle.
S1.do: Carries on and tries to save a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after families going through layoffs, and fund childcare properly so parents can retrain. That's where my union would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's fine. But parents losing jobs might pull kids out to save money, and our numbers drop. And the AI apps for little kids would be everywhere. That's what really worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to my director about keeping places for kids whose parents lose work, maybe on lower fees. Keep pushing the screen-free message with parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, more for the families.

S2.say: Look after families going through layoffs and fund childcare properly so parents can retrain.
S2.think: Her job is fine, but parents might pull children out to save money, and AI apps for small children would be everywhere.
S2.do: Asks her director about lower-fee places for children of laid-off parents and keeps pushing screen-free play.
S2.feel: A bit worried, more for the families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong that house prices boom while families lose their jobs. The gains should pay for things like childcare, schools and decent pay for carers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Physical jobs are untouched, so I'm still needed. But we rent, and booming house prices mean the rent goes up. With a little one and almost no savings, that's the scary part, not the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'we rent'. Is buying something you'd still hope for in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. I'd let that dream go. I'd just want a lease that doesn't jump every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask for a pay rise, or move to a better-paid centre, because there'd be plenty of work. Talk with my partner about moving somewhere cheaper. Join the union campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe at work. Squeezed at home.

S3.say: It's wrong that house prices boom while families lose jobs. The gains should pay for childcare, schools and carers.
S3.think: She's still needed, but booming prices push up the rent, and with a child and almost no savings that's the scary part.
S3.do: Asks for a raise or moves to a better-paid centre, talks about moving somewhere cheaper and joins the union campaign.
S3.feel: Safe at work, squeezed at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, absolutely not with small children. A robot can't love a child. I'd say that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care homes on your list surprised me. If they put robots there, someone will try it in nurseries to save money. I don't think parents would accept it for little ones. I hope not. I'm good at my job, but good doesn't always win against cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get involved with the union and the parents' groups early, to push for rules on robots around young children. Keep saving whatever I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. The first time this has felt close.

S4.say: Absolutely not with small children. A robot can't love a child.
S4.think: If robots go into care homes, someone will try them in nurseries to save money. She hopes parents refuse, but good doesn't always beat cheap.
S4.do: Works early with her union and parents' groups to push for rules on robots around young children, and keeps saving.
S4.feel: Shaken. The first time it has felt close.
